text: Defender for Endpoint watches devices, Defender for Office 365 watches email, and Defender for Cloud Apps watches SaaS usage — all three cloud-facing in one way or another. None of them watches the on-prem Active Directory domain controller almost every enterprise still depends on for authentication. Defender for Identity exists specifically to close that gap.

Defender for Identity deploys a sensor directly on domain controllers and AD FS servers, analyzing authentication traffic, network traffic, and Windows event logs from the one vantage point that can actually see what's happening to on-prem identity — not from the cloud, but right on the DC itself.

Pass-the-Hash abuses the fact that Windows can authenticate using a password's NTLM hash directly, without needing the plaintext password. An attacker who compromised one machine extracts a cached hash and authenticates to another machine with it — lateral movement that looks like a normal login to anything not specifically watching for it.

Golden Ticket goes further: Kerberos relies on the KRBTGT account to sign ticket-granting tickets, and an attacker who steals that account's password hash can forge their own tickets offline, valid for whatever accounts and lifetimes they choose, bypassing normal authentication entirely.

DCSync abuses the same replication protocol domain controllers normally use to sync data, including password hashes, with each other. An attacker with enough replication rights impersonates a DC and requests a replication of password hashes for any account in the domain — a request an ordinary workstation never legitimately makes.

Pass-the-Hash, Golden Ticket, and DCSync are all attacks against on-prem identity infrastructure that Defender for Endpoint, Office 365, and Cloud Apps were never positioned to see. Each Defender XDR workload watches a different piece of the environment, and Defender for Identity is the piece that watches on-prem identity — the gap none of the other three could have closed on their own.
